property_summary: For every state of the contract, owner() returns the stored owner address (i.e. the canonical owner getter returns the same value as the internal _owner storage); the mutant changes behavior when _owner == address(0) by still returning address(0) (no functional change normally) but the intended rule is that owner() should always return the actual stored _owner value — the mutant introduces a divergent code path that can be observed by setting owner to address(0) and calling owner().

For every input, the deployed reference contract's owner() returns the actual stored owner value (including when owner is zero after transfer), whereas the mutant returns address(0) whenever the internal owner storage is zero which can change the returned value for some inputs.

For every address X that may be set as the contract owner via transferOwnership, the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner value; the mutant incorrectly maps a stored zero owner to address(0) via a conditional branch, so when owner is set to address(0) (by transferOwnership to zero), the mutant's owner() can differ — the test fuzzes a candidate newOwner and asserts owner() equals the stored expectation after calling transferOwnership (using only public surface).

For any address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the public owner() getter returns exactly newOwner (the stored owner); the mutant adds a conditional that can make owner() return address(0) when the stored owner is address(0), breaking the equivalence for some fuzzed newOwner (specifically when newOwner == address(0)).

For every fuzzed candidate address newOwner, after calling setUp-deployed contract's transferOwnership(newOwner) from the current owner, the public owner() getter returns the stored owner value (i.e. equals newOwner); the mutant's added branch changes observable return when the stored owner equals address(0) causing owner() to behave differently for some fuzzed newOwner (address(0)).

For any nonzero candidate newOwner address, transferOwnership called by the current owner succeeds; the buggy mutant additionally allows transferring ownership to the zero address, which the reference disallows — thus calling transferOwnership with address(0) should revert on the reference but succeed on the mutant.

For any caller, calling transferOwnership(address) when called by the contract owner must revert if the newOwner is the zero address; the mutant that removed that require allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed (violating this rule).

For every address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) from the current owner never succeeds when newOwner == address(0) (reference reverts); the mutant removed that check and thus allows transfer to address(0), so the property is that transferOwnership(address(0)) must revert when called by the owner.

For any caller who is the owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert if newOwner is the zero address (reference enforces this); the mutant removed that check and thus allows transferring ownership to address(0), violating the rule for some input (newOwner = address(0)).

For all addresses newOwner, when called by the current owner transferOwnership(newOwner) must NOT succeed if newOwner is a contract that reverts during OwnershipTransferred event emission (i.e., transferring ownership must revert if the newOwner is an address(0) replacement that causes ownership transfer mechanics to fail); the mutant that removes the require allows transferring ownership to problematic addresses and thus can change owner when the reference would revert.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (returns without revert) for all non-zero newOwner addresses including when newOwner == owner; the mutant wrongly rejects calls where newOwner == owner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address (non-zero), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds (does not revert); the mutant adds a require forbidding transferring ownership to the same owner so calls where newOwner == owner will revert (breaking the rule).

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address that is non-zero, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds (i.e. does not revert); the mutant adds a require forbidding transferring ownership to the same owner so calls with newOwner == owner will revert, violating this property for those inputs.

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address (including the owner's own address), transferOwnership(newOwner) does not revert; the mutant adds a require forbidding transferring ownership to the same address, so calls where newOwner == owner will revert.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any newOwner address that is non-zero, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference always succeeds (does not revert); the mutant adds a require forbidding transferring ownership to the same current owner, so when newOwner == owner the mutant will revert and thus violate this property for those inputs.

Rule: Only the contract owner (owner() == msg.sender) can successfully call transferOwnership(address) — the reference enforces this for every caller, while the mutant that uses tx.origin allows an attacker to cause transferOwnership to succeed when forwarded through a contract (tx.origin != msg.sender), breaking the rule for some inputs.
